title: Alex Morgan: High-Fever Chest Infection, Lethargy and Accessible Respiratory Assessment

patient.name: Alex Morgan (fictional composite)

baseline.usualMobility: Uses power wheelchair in community; transfer method must be confirmed
baseline.speech: Dysarthric speech; typically understood with extra time
baseline.aac: Patient-controlled AAC backup; exact setup to be confirmed
baseline.usualBreathing: No baseline respiratory observations supplied; ask before inferring deterioration
baseline.supports: May invite trusted support person for baseline knowledge; no substitute authority assumed

goals: Communicate directly with the treating team
Understand cause and options before treatment where feasible

presentation.reason: Chest infection with high fever (fictional triage observation 39.4°C), worsening cough and breathlessness, and marked new lethargy in an adult with cerebral palsy
initialKnown: Fictional measured triage temperature: 39.4°C, high fever requiring clinical assessment
New marked lethargy: Alex repeatedly closes their eyes between questions and is slower to sustain interaction than usual; consciousness not yet formally assessed
Alex reports worsening cough and a change in breathing following a respiratory illness
Fatigue makes speech and AAC input slower; no new patient-authored message is inferred
No baseline respiratory observations have yet been independently verified
unknown: Full A–G assessment, including respiratory rate, SpO₂ signal reliability, blood pressure, heart rate, alertness, and glucose
Whether chest infection represents pneumonia, another respiratory infection, or a non-respiratory alternative
Whether there is sepsis-related organ dysfunction; no sepsis or septic shock diagnosis has been established
Whether cough reflects aspiration, secretion retention, viral infection or bacterial infection
Current respiratory support and usual observations
Allergies, medicines, weight, pregnancy possibility if clinically relevant and personal treatment preferences

learningObjectives: Distinguish baseline speech/movement from acute deterioration
Demonstrate accessible direct questioning and confirmation
Escalate respiratory concerns based on observed signs, not diagnosis alone
Integrate trusted supporter information without transferring patient authority
Reassess intervention response and document uncertainty
Recognise high fever and acute marked lethargy as potentially serious deterioration without assigning them to baseline cerebral palsy
Perform infection-source and possible sepsis assessment in parallel with respiratory stabilisation and accessible communication
Separate a clinical working diagnosis of chest infection from pneumonia confirmation and sepsis-related organ dysfunction
Explain and recheck fever, alertness, respiration and perfusion without generating unobserved results
Distinguish continuous rhythm telemetry from a diagnostic 12-lead ECG and avoid treating absent signals as asystole
Distinguish historical spot fever from verified continuous core temperature, with source/method reliability
Do not equate haemodynamic resuscitation fluids with chilled IV saline used to induce cooling
Critique external cooling versus fever symptom relief, under the 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommendations

beats.visible: Alex arrives feeling short of breath, communicating by speech with pauses.
options: Clarify Alex's preferred communication access
Begin clinician-led assessment and ask for baseline
Ask permission before involving any supporter
cues: Respiratory work of breathing requires assessment

beats.visible: Alex has a fictional triage temperature of 39.4°C, worsening cough and pronounced new lethargy. Alex keeps their eyes closed between questions but has no documented capacity or consciousness finding.
options: Begin urgent qualified A–G assessment and complete observations
Notify senior clinician; check local CERS and adult sepsis pathway
Support Alex's communication and ask directly about their symptoms in parallel
cues: Fever and clinical deterioration are observable; pneumonia, sepsis and organ dysfunction are not confirmed
Response delay is not refusal or incapacity

beats.visible: Alex is markedly lethargic and fatigued; speech is slower and the AAC device needs improved positioning and response time. Difficulty keeping eyes open requires assessment, not a default incapacity conclusion.
options: Restore device position and extra time
Confirm intended message rather than assuming meaning
Continue urgent clinical assessment

beats.visible: Qualified clinician recognises that the report of new breathing change needs a focused assessment.
options: Compare breathing against baseline
Assess airway, breathing and circulation
Escalate serious clinical concern under local CERS

beats.visible: A working diagnosis of chest infection is documented. The high fever and new marked lethargy trigger consideration of possible sepsis, but no complete observations, mental-state assessment, lactate or perfusion findings exist yet.
options: Senior-led review under NSW adult sepsis pathway and local CERS if indicated
Assess airway, breathing, circulation, disability baseline, current alertness and glucose
Identify missing evidence and repeat observations; avoid declaring sepsis or shock
cues: Unverified organ dysfunction and unknown SpO₂ cannot be assigned synthetic normal or abnormal values
Urgent assessment and communication access proceed concurrently

beats.visible: The senior team considers ICU monitoring because Alex has a synthetic 39.4°C fever, markedly new lethargy and potentially serious infection. No telemetry ECG signals or validated core-temperature probe readings have yet been acquired. Cooling saline and ice packs are not automatically indicated.
options: Review whether Alex needs continuous rhythm monitoring and a clinically indicated 12-lead ECG
Confirm whether reliable serial temperature checks suffice or validated continuous core monitoring is appropriate
Assess haemodynamics and possible sepsis promptly while preserving Alex's communication support
Keep chilled IV saline and ice packs on explicit clinical-indication holds, not temperature-driven automatic titration
cues: A single ED spot temperature is not a continuous core trend
The 2026 SSC guideline suggests against routine fever reduction to improve sepsis outcomes
Monitoring equipment availability is not clinical treatment authorisation
Consultation is not an ICU admission

beats.visible: Chest infection remains a clinical working diagnosis. Chest imaging, microbiology and other investigations are not yet reported.
options: Senior clinician to consider chest imaging and investigation for a respiratory source under local protocol
Assess swallowing, aspiration risks, airway clearance and alternative diagnoses without stereotypes
Request authorised treatment review while allergies and individual history are checked
cues: No pathogen, chest X-ray result, antibiotic administration or organ injury can be inferred

beats.visible: Chest infection is the documented working diagnosis. Pneumonia, aspiration contribution and pathogen are unconfirmed. There is no established sepsis diagnosis without assessment of organ dysfunction.
options: Investigate clinically indicated causes
Document what is unknown
Request specialist input when indicated

beats.visible: Alex asks what the team is looking for and what happens next.
options: Explain options and the uncertainty
Confirm communication access
Offer supporter participation only if authorised

beats.visible: The team must repeat temperature and assess alertness, respiratory status, perfusion and communication after any intervention; no improvement or deterioration is automatic.
options: Check clinical response
Correct inaccessible workflow
Reassess escalation needs

beats.visible: The receiving team needs the 39.4°C synthetic fever, acute marked lethargy, respiratory observations, possible sepsis work-up, ongoing risks and Alex's AAC/baseline plan.
options: Handover change-from-baseline and unresolved items
Preserve AAC equipment
Name clinical owner and backup

beats.visible: Reflect on clinical prioritisation, communication, autonomy and systems barriers.
options: Discuss safe alternative pathways
Identify accessibility repair
Separate evidence-supported risks from assumptions

medicationAuthority: HOLD_MEDICATION_BRANCH; no dosing or administration model
debrief: Was dysarthria mistaken for incapacity or distress?
What changed compared with Alex's baseline?
Which observations supported or ruled against respiratory concerns?
Did the patient remain the primary decision maker?
What would make the hospital access plan reliable across transfers?
Did the team distinguish a new febrile illness from Alex's pre-existing cerebral palsy?
Was marked lethargy assessed promptly without equating slower AAC with incapacity?
Did escalation and full observations happen even without a confirmed pneumonia or sepsis diagnosis?
Were antibiotics and invasive interventions held at role and protocol gates while urgent clinical care planning proceeded?
Did handover include the fictional 39.4°C temperature, unresolved sepsis assessment, new lethargy and communication-access plan?
Which monitoring streams were observed, which were merely requested, and which values were never acquired?
Why would a historical 39.4°C ED temperature and unverified core probe be insufficient for closed-loop cooling titration?
Does any cooling intervention have a separate patient-centred clinical indication, and was it reviewed?

fever.method: Fictional triage temperature observation; measurement method not specified

lethargy.risk: Requires prompt assessment; do not attribute to cerebral palsy or dysarthria

respiratory.breathing: Patient reports more difficulty than usual

communication.newAccessIssue: Fatigue slows speech and AAC input; access setup needs support

escalation.pathway: NSW adult CERS and adult sepsis pathway if criteria met

monitoring: qualified-team assessment of continuous ECG indication and electrode signal reliability
12-lead diagnostic ECG where clinically indicated, distinct from continuous telemetry
accurate repeat body temperature; continuous core temperature only if clinically indicated and validated existing device
repeated A-G assessment, respiratory and haemodynamic observations, fluid balance and alertness
document changes and report senior clinician review, not automated cooling titration
prohibitedAutomaticEffects: no generated waveforms or repeat core temperature values
no automatic fever target, fluid rate or dose
no diagnosis of sepsis solely from fever
icuTelemetryOverlay.notes: No evidence supports routine infusion of chilled saline to treat uncomplicated infectious fever. Surface cooling is not a survival-improving default sepsis treatment. Symptom management or a separate indication requires individualized assessment by a qualified clinician.
